quotes.quote: Refusal is only one third of willpower. When a lapse repeats, ask which power went quiet before you call yourself weak.
quotes.why: This is the chapter's clearest, most memorable reframing.

quotes.quote: A goal must be present to have power.
quotes.why: Short line that captures the mechanism behind the whole lesson.

quotes.quote: Weekly practice: For the first half of this week, use your usual all-or-nothing rule. For the second half, swap in the Three-Power Check and compare which half made the next action clearer.
quotes.why: The comparison task is more artificial than the otherwise low-friction advice.

quotes.quote: b) The saving goal must be fake whenever opening the sale tab feels relieving.
quotes.why: This distractor is so extreme that it weakens the quiz as evidence of understanding.

tells: Several wrong answers are guessable because they use absolutes or cartoon claims such as 'only,' 'fake,' 'no value,' and 'avoid cooperation.'
Q1's correct answer closely mirrors the chapter's exact three-part formula, while the distractors are narrower or moralizing.

complaints.problem: Several distractors are implausibly absolute or moralizing, letting a reader eliminate them without relying much on the prose.
The correct option repeats the chapter's three-part formula almost verbatim, making the item easier than it needs to be.
Thin-but-usable example: it names the cue and value but gives little before-to-after consequence after Brooklyn names the running goal.
The repeated Miller/Cohen explanation makes several transfer examples feel formulaic rather than distinct.
Asking readers to spend half the week using the weaker all-or-nothing rule is a slightly theatrical comparison exercise, not the chapter's most practical move.

parsedReview.oneParagraphVerdict: This is a strong opening chapter: the core move is memorable, concrete, and well explained through the three-power frame, with enough brain mechanism to make it feel grounded without becoming technical. The quizzes are fair and derivable, but too many distractors are obvious straw choices, so the assessment under-measures real comprehension. Transfer is usable across spending, food, anger, clinical work, and family obligations, though a few examples repeat the same explanatory beat. No must-fix reader-harming defects appear; it ships, with quiz sharpening as the main improvement.
